svg.title: What a deployment rollback restores, and what it leaves exactly where it is
svg.desc: Under a header naming the Deployment object and the single JSON Patch operation that rolls it back, a replace of the path slash spec slash template sent as application slash json-patch plus json, two columns of identical width divide the change into five rows each, set on the same baselines. The left column, headed Restored and ticked, covers everything under spec dot template: container images for every container and every init container, command and arguments and environment variables including valueFrom references, resource requests and limits and all three kinds of probe, volumes and mounts and security context and service account name, and the template's own labels and annotations along with every other field under spec dot template. The right column, headed Not restored and crossed, covers what is left exactly where it is: spec dot replicas, which lives outside the template and is left alone even if something scaled it mid-incident; deployment-level fields such as the rollout strategy, minimum ready seconds and the progress deadline; labels and annotations on the Deployment object itself; objects the template only references, including config maps, secrets, persistent volume claims, services and any horizontal pod autoscaler; and anything changed outside this Deployment, which is most of what a bad deploy actually touches. The two columns are drawn the same size on purpose, because the second is not a footnote to the first. A band across the bottom shows that both lists, and a warning naming the replica count that was left behind, are returned on every rollback whether it was applied or refused, so a caller cannot close the incident on a partial fix.
